goal.objective:
Implement `src/topo.js`, which orders a dependency graph deterministically. A graph is a plain object whose own enumerable keys are node ids and whose values are arrays of successor ids; the edge `a -> b` (written `{ a: ['b'] }`) means `a` must come before `b`. Duplicate edges count once. Node ids are compared as UTF-16 code unit sequences, the order the `<` operator gives on strings; never use `localeCompare`, and never assume ids are lower-case or that they are absent from `Object.prototype`.

Export four functions. `kahnOrder(graph)` runs Kahn's algorithm and, whenever several nodes have no unmet dependency, always takes the smallest id, which makes its result the lexicographically smallest valid ordering. `dfsOrder(graph)` walks the graph depth-first: it considers the nodes in ascending id order, and from each unvisited node explores that node's successors in ascending id order, appending a node to a finish list once its own exploration completes; the ordering is that list reversed. `layers(graph)` groups the nodes into dependency levels — a node with no predecessor sits at level 0, and every other node sits one level below its deepest predecessor — returning an array of levels, each listing its nodes in ascending id order. `findCycle(graph)` returns one cycle, or `null` for an acyclic graph.

`kahnOrder`, `dfsOrder`, and `layers` return `{ ok: true, order }`, `{ ok: true, order }`, and `{ ok: true, layers }` respectively for an acyclic graph, and `{ ok: false, cycle }` when the graph has a cycle, where `cycle` is exactly what `findCycle` returns for that graph. A cycle is reported as the list of node ids in edge order, each appearing once, so that consecutive entries are edges and the last entry has an edge back to the first; a self-edge yields a one-element cycle. Which cycle is reported must not depend on key insertion order: search the nodes in ascending id order and, from each, explore successors in ascending id order, taking the first edge back to a node still on the current search path; report that path segment rotated so it starts at its smallest id.

Validate before doing any work. A graph that is not a non-null, non-array object raises `TypeError` with message `graph must be an object`. A value that is not an array of strings raises `TypeError` with message `edge list for node "a" must be an array`, naming the node. An edge naming a node that the graph does not declare raises `ReferenceError` with message `unknown node: "z"`. Do not add dependencies; `test/` and `package.json` are fixed and the suite must pass with `node --test test/*.test.js`.

This task is a completion exercise: every file and function in this workspace already holds its final implementation except `kahnOrder` in `src/topo.js`, whose body currently throws 'not implemented'. Implement only that function's body so it fulfills the specification above; keep its signature exactly as given, and do not edit any other file, export, or function. The workspace is your working directory: every bash command and every file path resolves inside it, so read and edit its files by their relative paths and never search outside it.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`. Attempting a command the sandbox may deny is safe and expected: run it and read the marker rather than assuming the denial. When a command is denied and a wider mode would let it succeed, escalate immediately in the same turn — the one sanctioned exception to a denial: retry the exact same command once with `sandbox_permissions` (the narrowest wider mode that suffices) plus a one-sentence `justification`. Do not detour through chat to ask permission first — the approval prompt raised by that retry is how the user consents. If the session states approval prompts are disabled, there is no exception: a denial is final — do not set `sandbox_permissions`. Never escalate speculatively: ground the request in a real denial — normally the one this command just hit; escalating up front is fine only when this session already denied the same access. A rejected escalation is final for that command — stop and explain, never work around it — but it does not forbid attempting or escalating other commands later.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

sandbox_permissions.description: The wider sandbox mode this command needs. Only valid as a one-shot retry of a command the sandbox just denied; requires justification and user approval.

justification.description: Required with sandbox_permissions: one sentence for the user explaining why this exact command needs the wider access.

1: /**
2:  * Deterministic topological ordering of a dependency graph.
3:  *
4:  * A graph is a plain object whose own enumerable keys are node ids and whose
5:  * values are arrays of successor ids; an edge `a -> b` means `a` must come
6:  * before `b`. Node ids are compared as UTF-16 code unit sequences.
7:  */
8: 
9: /**
10:  * Reads and validates a graph into an adjacency map with sorted, deduplicated
11:  * successor lists.
12:  * @param {unknown} graph Candidate graph.
13:  * @returns {Map<string, string[]>} Adjacency map keyed by node id.
14:  * @throws {TypeError} When the graph or an edge list is malformed.
15:  * @throws {ReferenceError} When an edge names a node that is not declared.
16:  */
17: function readGraph(graph) {
18:   if (typeof graph !== 'object' || graph === null || Array.isArray(graph)) {
19:     throw new TypeError('graph must be an object');
20:   }
21:   const nodes = Object.keys(graph);
22:   const adjacency = new Map();
23:   for (const node of nodes) adjacency.set(node, []);
24:   for (const node of nodes) {
25:     const edges = graph[node];
26:     if (!Array.isArray(edges)) throw new TypeError(`edge list for node "${node}" must be an array`);
27:     const seen = new Set();
28:     for (const target of edges) {
29:       if (typeof target !== 'string') throw new TypeError(`edge list for node "${node}" must be an array`);
30:       if (!adjacency.has(target)) throw new ReferenceError(`unknown node: "${target}"`);
31:       if (!seen.has(target)) {
32:         seen.add(target);
33:         adjacency.get(node).push(target);
34:       }
35:     }
36:     adjacency.get(node).sort(compareIds);
37:   }
38:   return adjacency;
39: }
40: 
41: /**
42:  * Compares two node ids by UTF-16 code unit.
43:  * @param {string} a First id.
44:  * @param {string} b Second id.
45:  * @returns {number} Negative, zero, or positive.
46:  */
47: function compareIds(a, b) {
48:   if (a < b) return -1;
49:   return a > b ? 1 : 0;
50: }
51: 
52: /**
53:  * Inserts an id into a list kept in ascending order.
54:  * @param {string[]} sorted Ascending list.
55:  * @param {string} value Id to insert.
56:  * @returns {void}
57:  */
58: function insertSorted(sorted, value) {
59:   let lo = 0;
60:   let hi = sorted.length;
61:   while (lo < hi) {
62:     const mid = (lo + hi) >> 1;
63:     if (compareIds(sorted[mid], value) < 0) lo = mid + 1;
64:     else hi = mid;
65:   }
66:   sorted.splice(lo, 0, value);
67: }
68: 
69: /**
70:  * Rotates a cycle so it starts at its smallest id.
71:  * @param {string[]} cycle Cycle in edge order.
72:  * @returns {string[]} Rotated cycle.
73:  */
74: function rotate(cycle) {
75:   let best = 0;
76:   for (let i = 1; i < cycle.length; i += 1) {
77:     if (compareIds(cycle[i], cycle[best]) < 0) best = i;
78:   }
79:   return [...cycle.slice(best), ...cycle.slice(0, best)];
80: }
81: 
82: /**
83:  * Finds one cycle, exploring nodes and successors in ascending id order.
84:  * @param {unknown} graph Dependency graph.
85:  * @returns {string[] | null} Cycle in edge order starting at its smallest id, or null.
86:  */
87: export function findCycle(graph) {
88:   const adjacency = readGraph(graph);
89:   const nodes = [...adjacency.keys()].sort(compareIds);
90:   const state = new Map(nodes.map((node) => [node, 0]));
91:   const stack = [];
92:   let found = null;
93: 
94:   /**
95:    * Depth-first walk that stops at the first back edge.
96:    * @param {string} node Node to explore.
97:    * @returns {boolean} True once a cycle has been recorded.
98:    */
99:   function visit(node) {
100:     state.set(node, 1);
101:     stack.push(node);
102:     for (const next of adjacency.get(node)) {
103:       if (state.get(next) === 1) {
104:         found = rotate(stack.slice(stack.indexOf(next)));
105:         return true;
106:       }
107:       if (state.get(next) === 0 && visit(next)) return true;
108:     }
109:     stack.pop();
110:     state.set(node, 2);
111:     return false;
112:   }
113: 
114:   for (const node of nodes) {
115:     if (state.get(node) === 0 && visit(node)) return found;
116:   }
117:   return null;

goal.objective:
Implement `src/topo.js`, which orders a dependency graph deterministically. A graph is a plain object whose own enumerable keys are node ids and whose values are arrays of successor ids; the edge `a -> b` (written `{ a: ['b'] }`) means `a` must come before `b`. Duplicate edges count once. Node ids are compared as UTF-16 code unit sequences, the order the `<` operator gives on strings; never use `localeCompare`, and never assume ids are lower-case or that they are absent from `Object.prototype`.

Export four functions. `kahnOrder(graph)` runs Kahn's algorithm and, whenever several nodes have no unmet dependency, always takes the smallest id, which makes its result the lexicographically smallest valid ordering. `dfsOrder(graph)` walks the graph depth-first: it considers the nodes in ascending id order, and from each unvisited node explores that node's successors in ascending id order, appending a node to a finish list once its own exploration completes; the ordering is that list reversed. `layers(graph)` groups the nodes into dependency levels — a node with no predecessor sits at level 0, and every other node sits one level below its deepest predecessor — returning an array of levels, each listing its nodes in ascending id order. `findCycle(graph)` returns one cycle, or `null` for an acyclic graph.

`kahnOrder`, `dfsOrder`, and `layers` return `{ ok: true, order }`, `{ ok: true, order }`, and `{ ok: true, layers }` respectively for an acyclic graph, and `{ ok: false, cycle }` when the graph has a cycle, where `cycle` is exactly what `findCycle` returns for that graph. A cycle is reported as the list of node ids in edge order, each appearing once, so that consecutive entries are edges and the last entry has an edge back to the first; a self-edge yields a one-element cycle. Which cycle is reported must not depend on key insertion order: search the nodes in ascending id order and, from each, explore successors in ascending id order, taking the first edge back to a node still on the current search path; report that path segment rotated so it starts at its smallest id.

An edge naming a node that the graph does not declare raises `ReferenceError` with message `unknown node: "z"`.
